074508ec114f8975.t: You may wonder whether filtering on the device makes the measurement itself heavier. The filtering runs on a dedicated thread, and the main thread only checks how the data grows and reads the GC counter. As described above, the contents of most blocks are not read, so the processing for filtering is limited to a small part of the data. The filtering thread and the Dispatcher thread that writes out Profiler data are identified by thread name and excluded from the output. The filtering processing is also excluded from Deep Profiling. If it were included, every method call in the filtering thread would become a sample and be written into the very raw log being read. However, the GC counter is a process-wide value, so it includes the several KB per frame that the filtering thread allocates. This is sufficiently small compared with the thresholds described below, but including the load of enabling the Profiler itself, we cannot say the measurement adds no overhead at all.

17ac70dd7f2c2fd5.t: In modern graphics APIs, the unit compiled at draw time is called a Pipeline State Object (PSO). A PSO is an object in which the GPU driver compiles a shader variant together with rendering settings (vertex layout, render pass attachments such as color format and MSAA, blend state, depth test, and stencil state) into GPU machine instructions. Generated PSOs are cached on the device and reused for the same rendering settings. In other words, even for the same shader variant, different rendering settings are compiled as separate PSOs.

It is a technique that bakes the vertex deformation data of an animation into a texture in advance and plays it back by reading the texture in the vertex shader. This time uses the same clock as the time recorded at the frame delimiters in the raw log. 50363e18e5445d8c.t: The biggest change in Unity is in rendering. With Render Graph introduced to URP in Unity 6, the focus of optimization work has shifted from rearranging commands yourself to correctly declaring resource usage to the engine and verifying the result. The Unity 6 generation also adds new options for shader warmup and for passing per-object parameters. On the C# side, little changes within Unity 6, but Unity 7 introduces CoreCLR to the Editor and some desktop players, and the garbage collection mechanism also changes significantly. Mobile, on the other hand, will stay on IL2CPP and the Boehm GC for the time being, so the existing approach to memory optimization remains valid. Around build and distribution, there are more settings that let you adjust the balance of size, memory, and speed without rewriting code.

61c1feb171136b25.t: As the patrol gets longer, where to put the raw log also becomes a problem. The SDK switches the raw log output destination at fixed sizes and splits it into sequentially numbered files, and the filtering thread deletes files it has finished reading. As a result, the device's storage usage plateaus at a few files. If filtering falls behind and too many unprocessed files accumulate, recording is stopped. When switching files, Unity rewrites all definitions of sampler names and object names that have appeared so far at the beginning of the new file. The output is concatenated into one file, so most definitions from the second file onward are duplicates. Definitions that are byte-for-byte identical to the one written immediately before are therefore omitted from the output. The output file has an upper limit of 1.5 GB, and recording stops when the next frame to keep would exceed the limit. Uploads are limited to 2 GB, so stopping before that ensures that the frames kept up to the limit are reliably sent.

Its defining feature is that it can greatly reduce draw calls, and compared with a configuration that has a Renderer per fragment, it was substantially more efficient, along with the Skin method. The two involve trade-offs: the Skin method is better in GPU time, and the VAT method is better in CPU time and memory. VAT is the first candidate for configurations with few passes that perform vertex calculations, or when the goal is to reduce CPU load. It has constraints such as the need to prepare dedicated assets and fixed motion, but it is a powerful option when a large number of objects play a predetermined animation.

698aaf21a06cc321.t: Some rules that grep cannot express are marked MANUAL on the checklist and are read closely only when they apply to the target type. Rules where the absence of a required statement is the condition for a finding are marked ABSENT, and their details are checked when grep produces no hit (this is explicit so that the correspondence between hits and finding conditions is not inverted). The primary scan was made a script because having an LLM run dozens of greps one by one can lead to skipped items, and differences in regular expression dialects (for example, PCRE lookahead does not work in the standard macOS grep) make results environment-dependent. This decouples the completeness of the primary scan from the model's memory. The correctness of findings (excluding false positives in the secondary review) remains the agent's judgment. Only the checklists are read in advance (about 16KB for code and about 8KB for assets; the token count depends on the model, but roughly 10,000 tokens in total), and details are read only for the hits. Because the checklists are generated automatically from the rule bodies, adding a rule requires no manual synchronization.

bf67ec17f15f3df4.t: The raw log is made by appending per-thread buffers in block units in sequence. To know which block belongs to which frame, you need to find the frame delimiters. The clue is how the Profiler writes. The Profiler switches the thread buffer immediately before and after writing a frame delimiter, so the delimiter arrives as a standalone block of only a dozen or so bytes. The filtering thread therefore opens only blocks no longer than this length and checks whether each is a delimiter. It does not read the contents of longer blocks and treats them as belonging to the current frame of that thread. When the next frame delimiter arrives on the main thread, the frame length is determined, so it decides there whether to keep the frame, and writes out only the blocks of frames to keep, in their original order. Definition blocks that belong to no frame, such as sampler names and thread names, are all written out, so the output can be opened as is in Unity's Profiler window.

Even for models without prepared LODs, a single setting reduces the polygon count at a distance and lowers GPU load. If you already use LOD Group, the polygon reduction effect is the same, and the difference is in memory. Mesh LOD adds no vertices; all LODs share the vertex buffer of the original mesh, and only the index buffer increases. fbaa9f3a7a77cc92.t: First, the CoreCLR GC is a @<b>{generational GC}. A generational GC manages allocated objects in groups called "generations". Newly allocated objects are first treated as gen0. GC on gen0 runs relatively frequently, but objects that survive a gen0 GC move to the next generation, gen1, where GC runs less frequently than for gen0. This is based on the general observation that most newly allocated objects are short-lived, while objects that have survived to some extent often survive for a long time afterward, and it aims to shorten the time taken by the frequent GCs on young generations. For memory optimization with the CoreCLR GC, which generation an allocated object belongs to and when the GC for each generation runs will be important points.
